VIDEO.title: The Hidden Clue in the Olivet Discourse (REVEALED)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 24:1-35 · Episode 46 (#49 of 58 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 24:1-35. As Jesus leaves the temple, the disciples point out its buildings, and He says not one stone will be left upon another. On the Mount of Olives they ask: 'when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?' Jesus warns of deceivers, wars, famines and earthquakes ('the beginning of birth pains'), persecution, and the abomination of desolation; those in Judea must flee to the mountains. After the tribulation come cosmic signs and the Son of Man coming on the clouds. Learn from the fig tree: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.

This begins Jesus' fifth and final discourse, on judgment (chapters 24 and 25); the video sees the five discourses as paralleling the five books of the Torah. Christians are divided over this passage.

The key is the disciples' question. It follows straight from 23:35-39, the judgment on the leaders, the city and the temple. The video reads it as one question about one event: many Jews spoke of this age and the age to come, and the disciples, picturing Daniel 7:13-14, linked the temple's fall with Jesus' coming and the end of the corrupt age.

Jesus answers in the prophets' apocalyptic style, full of Old Testament allusions (Deuteronomy 13, Daniel 9, 11 and 12, Joel 2, Zechariah 14 and more). He keeps saying 'you.' Luke's parallel explains the abomination: 'when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies' (Luke 21:20). The video holds that the discourse is about the destruction of the temple in AD 70, while acknowledging that others disagree.
The lesson: if God's people will filter the events taking place around them through the lens of His word, they will have the discernment to understand His activity.
QUOTES: If God's people will filter the events taking place around them through the lens of his word, they will have the discernment to understand his activity.
What did the disciples think that Jesus meant?

LSB_QUOTES.text: Truly I say to you, not one stone here will be left upon another, which will not be torn down.
Tell us, when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?
Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will not pass away.

src.text: And coming out from the temple, Jesus was going along, and His disciples came up to point out the temple buildings to Him. And He answered and said to them, “Do you not see all these things? Truly I say to you, not one stone here will be left upon another, which will not be torn down.”

lines.text: Jesus has just said, 'your house is being left to you desolate' (23:38). Leaving the temple, He says it again: the buildings will be torn down.
A little shy of 40 years later the Romans sacked the city and the temple. Jesus was absolutely correct.
Herod's temple was still being finished; Josephus describes stones of enormous size.

left.text: Now as He was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to Him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?”

right.text: And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed.

lines.text: Many Jews spoke of two ages: this corrupt age, under Greek influence and Roman rule, and the age to come, the age of the Messiah. The disciples saw the temple's fall as the end of this age.
That is why Peter rebuked Jesus (16:22), James and John asked for seats (20:21), and John asked from prison (Luke 7:19): they expected a kingdom of military dominance.

The Mishnah keeps both ages: 'this world is like a vestibule before the world to come' (Pirkei Avot 4:16), and 'The days of your life, refers to the days in this world, all is added to include the days of the Messiah' (Mishnah Berakhot 1:5).

src.text: And you are going to hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for those things must take place, but that is not yet the end. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and in various places there will be famines and earthquakes. But all these things are merely the beginning of birth pains.

lines.text: Why not just say, 'In 37 years, on a Tuesday at 3:00 p.m., the Romans will destroy the temple'? Because the prophets spoke in layered images that connect back to God's word. Prophecy communicates what God is saying and stands on what He has already spoken.

The video's chart: false messiahs (Deuteronomy 13; Jeremiah 23), wars (Isaiah 19; Ezekiel 38-39), the abomination (Daniel 9, 11, 12), fleeing to the mountains (Zechariah 14), cosmic signs (Isaiah 13; Joel 2).

left.text: “Therefore when you see the abomination of desolation which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains.

right.text: “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is at hand.

lines.text: Many today think of a future Antichrist in a rebuilt temple. Luke's account shows what the disciples heard: Jerusalem surrounded by the Roman army, which desolated the city and the temple in AD 70.
The phrase recalls Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple and offered pagan sacrifices there (Daniel 11:31).
Josephus says that as the sanctuary burned, the Romans brought their standards into the temple court and sacrificed to them (Jewish War 6.316).

SIGNS.title: Flee, and do not be deceived

src.text: Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or ‘There He is,’ do not believe him. For false christs and false prophets will arise and will show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have told you in advance. Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, He is in the wilderness,’ do not go out, or, ‘Behold, He is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe them.

lines.text: Two things stand out in Jesus' answer: events around the temple's fall would confuse many, so He warns against deceivers (24:4, 11, 24) and commands calm (24:6, 23, 26).
Second, the copious Old Testament allusions: to interpret prophecy, God's people need to know God's word.

left.text: “But immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

right.text: For the stars of heaven and their constellations / Will not flash forth their light; / The sun will be dark when it rises / And the moon will not shed its light.

lines.text: This is how Jewish prophets spoke about coming judgment. Isaiah used these images for the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:1, 10), Joel for the day of Yahweh (Joel 2:10).
The Son of Man 'coming on the clouds' (24:30) quotes Daniel 7:13, where one like a Son of Man comes up to the Ancient of Days.

src.text: “Now learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and puts forth its leaves, you know that summer is near; so, you too, when you see all these things, recognize that He is near, right at the door. Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.

lines.text: Jesus uses 'you' and 'your' again and again from 24:3 on: these things will happen to the disciples and their generation.
Jesus uses 'see' and 'look' repeatedly: 'when you see all these things.' Signs are for those who know God's word.

left.text: whom heaven must receive until the period of restoration of all things about which God spoke by the mouth of His holy prophets from ancient time.

right.text: and so all Israel will be saved; just as it is written, / “The Deliverer will come from Zion, / He will remove ungodliness from Jacob.”

lines.text: The video asks a Bible software study tool how first-century Jews understood the end of the age, then compares Peter's words on the restoration with Paul in Romans 11.
Paul's birth-pain image is in Romans 8:22: 'the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth together until now.'

FIG.title: See what the Father is doing

src.text: Therefore Jesus answered and was saying to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing from Himself, unless it is something He sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in the same manner.

lines.text: As God's adopted children, we should be able to survey our own circumstances and recognize the activity of God, through His word, and then go and be a part of it.
If God's people will filter the events taking place around them through the lens of His word, they will have the discernment to understand His activity.

BACKGROUND.p: The revolt against Rome began in AD 66. Vespasian subdued Galilee first; his son Titus besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, and the temple burned in the late summer of that year.

In 167 BC the Seleucid king stopped the sacrifices and defiled the temple with pagan worship. 1 Maccabees calls it a desolating sacrilege on the altar; the temple was cleansed and rededicated three years later.
Later rabbinic texts speak of 'this world' and 'the world to come,' and of 'the days of the Messiah' in between (Mishnah Berakhot 1:5; Pirkei Avot 4:16).

DEBATES.p: The video holds that the discourse is about the destruction of the temple in AD 70 (a preterist reading). Others read it as about the end of history, and many see both: the near event of AD 70 as a pattern of the final coming.
The video reads 24:3 as one question about one event. Others see two or three questions (the temple's fall; the coming; the end of the age), with Jesus answering each.
Many note five long discourses in Matthew, each ending 'when Jesus had finished' (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Whether they deliberately mirror the five books of Moses is debated.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The words about heaven receiving Jesus 'until the period of restoration of all things' are from Peter's sermon in Acts 3:21, not his epistle.
The labor-pain image the study tool attributes to Romans 11 is in Romans 8:22.
The sources for Antiochus describe pagan sacrifices and a 'desolating sacrilege' on the altar; the statue of Zeus is a later report.
Josephus places the Roman standards in the temple court while the sanctuary was burning, not after the temple was destroyed (Jewish War 6.316).
Counts of 'you' and 'see' depend on the translation; the LSB numbers differ slightly.

APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: if God's people will filter the events taking place around them through the lens of His word, they will have the discernment to understand His activity. Jesus spoke apocalyptically to send His disciples back to God's word, so they would know not only when the temple would fall, but why, and how to discern the moment. The same holds for us: like the Son who does what He sees the Father doing (John 5:19), we should survey our circumstances, recognize God's activity through His word, and go and be a part of it.

   This generation Matthew 24:32-34: "“Now learn the parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and puts forth its leaves, you know that summer is near; so, you too, when you see all these things, recognize that He is near, right at the door. Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+24:32-34
   (video) Jesus uses 'you' and 'your' again and again from 24:3 on: these things will happen to the disciples and their generation.
   (video) Jesus uses 'see' and 'look' repeatedly: 'when you see all these things.' Signs are for those who know God's word.
2. Acts 3:21; Romans 11:25-26: Following the rabbit trail
   Peter (Acts 3:21, LSB): "whom heaven must receive until the period of restoration of all things about which God spoke by the mouth of His holy prophets from ancient time."
   Paul (Romans 11:26, LSB): "and so all Israel will be saved; just as it is written, / “The Deliverer will come from Zion, / He will remove ungodliness from Jacob.”"
   (video) The video asks a Bible software study tool how first-century Jews understood the end of the age, then compares Peter's words on the restoration with Paul in Romans 11.
   [Background] Paul's birth-pain image is in Romans 8:22: 'the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth together until now.' (Romans 8:22)
3. John 5:19: See what the Father is doing
   Lesson John 5:19: "Therefore Jesus answered and was saying to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing from Himself, unless it is something He sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does in the same manner." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=John+5:19
   (video) As God's adopted children, we should be able to survey our own circumstances and recognize the activity of God, through His word, and then go and be a part of it.

## Key people
- The disciples: Point out the temple buildings, then ask one question about its fall. [Background] Mark 13:3 names Peter, James, John and Andrew.
- Daniel: The prophet of the Son of Man and the abomination of desolation. [Background] Jesus calls him 'Daniel the prophet' (24:15).
- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: Desecrated the temple before Jesus' day. [Background] Seleucid king; the temple was rededicated under the Maccabees, remembered at Hanukkah (John 10:22).
- The Romans: Surrounded Jerusalem and destroyed the temple in AD 70. [Background] Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, led the siege.
- Josephus: Says the Roman soldiers worshiped their standards in the temple. [Background] Jewish historian who witnessed the siege and wrote the Jewish War.

## Places [Background]
- Temple (named in the video): 'Not one stone here will be left upon another' (24:2).
- Mount of Olives (named in the video): Where Jesus sat with the disciples, facing the temple (24:3).
- Antonia Fortress: Roman garrison beside the temple; Titus's legions took it before the temple fell.

## Key terms
- Olivet Discourse: Jesus' teaching on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24-25), His fifth and last discourse.
- This age and the age to come: The Jewish hope that the Messiah would end this corrupt age and bring the age to come.
- Birth pains: Labor pains, an image of the troubles before God's new age (24:8).
- Abomination of desolation: Daniel's phrase for a desecration of the temple (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11).
- Apocalyptic: Revelatory language of cosmic signs and judgment, used by the prophets.
- Preterism: The view that much or all of the discourse was fulfilled in AD 70. [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The Jewish War: The revolt against Rome began in AD 66. Vespasian subdued Galilee first; his son Titus besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, and the temple burned in the late summer of that year.
- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: In 167 BC the Seleucid king stopped the sacrifices and defiled the temple with pagan worship. 1 Maccabees calls it a desolating sacrilege on the altar; the temple was cleansed and rededicated three years later.
- Two ages: Later rabbinic texts speak of 'this world' and 'the world to come,' and of 'the days of the Messiah' in between (Mishnah Berakhot 1:5; Pirkei Avot 4:16).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "And this gospel shall be preached in the whole world for a witness to all nations, and then shall the end come, of the downfall of Jerusalem." Homilies on Matthew 75, on 24:14. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Whence he seems to me to be speaking of the armies." Homilies on Matthew 76, on 24:15. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Peruse the history about these things composed by Josephus, and you will know all accurately." Homilies on Matthew 75, on 24:7. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- AD 70, the end, or both? The video holds that the discourse is about the destruction of the temple in AD 70 (a preterist reading). Others read it as about the end of history, and many see both: the near event of AD 70 as a pattern of the final coming.
- One question or several? The video reads 24:3 as one question about one event. Others see two or three questions (the temple's fall; the coming; the end of the age), with Jesus answering each.
- Five discourses like five books? Many note five long discourses in Matthew, each ending 'when Jesus had finished' (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Whether they deliberately mirror the five books of Moses is debated.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The words about heaven receiving Jesus 'until the period of restoration of all things' are from Peter's sermon in Acts 3:21, not his epistle.
- The labor-pain image the study tool attributes to Romans 11 is in Romans 8:22.
- The sources for Antiochus describe pagan sacrifices and a 'desolating sacrilege' on the altar; the statue of Zeus is a later report.
- Josephus places the Roman standards in the temple court while the sanctuary was burning, not after the temple was destroyed (Jewish War 6.316).
- Counts of 'you' and 'see' depend on the translation; the LSB numbers differ slightly.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What did the disciples most likely mean by 'the end of the age'?
2. Why does Jesus answer in images rather than dates?
3. How does Luke 21:20 help you read Matthew 24:15?
4. Which Old Testament passage behind this chapter would you like to study first?
5. Why does Jesus keep telling them not to be alarmed or deceived?
6. Where do you see God at work around you right now, and how does His word help you see it?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: if God's people will filter the events taking place around them through the lens of His word, they will have the discernment to understand His activity. Jesus spoke apocalyptically to send His disciples back to God's word, so they would know not only when the temple would fall, but why, and how to discern the moment. The same holds for us: like the Son who does what He sees the Father doing (John 5:19), we should survey our circumstances, recognize God's activity through His word, and go and be a part of it.
- Study note (added): pick one allusion from the video's chart this week, read the Old Testament passage in full, and note what it adds to Matthew 24.
